To initialize a generic object, give the generic class name followed by the type in angle brackets:
The type argument on the **right** may be omitted, leaving the empty **diamond operator**:

The **left** side declares the variable and its type: it is **required**, and it is what tells the compiler what `T` is. The **right** side may be shortened to `<>`, because the compiler infers the type from the left.

Gen<Integer> iData = new Gen<>();     // correct, diamond on the right
Gen iData = new Gen<Integer>();       // compiles, but Gen is now a "raw type", unchecked warnings
Notice `Gen<Integer>` rather than `Gen<int>`. **Type parameters must be reference types**: generics do not work with primitives. `Gen<int>` will not compile.

iData.setValue(1);              // autoboxing:   int 1  →  Integer.valueOf(1)
int num = iData.getValue();     // unboxing:     Integer →  int
Java converts automatically between primitives and their **wrapper classes**: `int`/`Integer`, `double`/`Double`, `char`/`Character`, `boolean`/`Boolean`. The example above relies on this.

First pair: 1 and One
Second pair: 7 and 25
Type parameter names are single capital letters by convention. A second parameter is usually **`V`** (Value) or `U`, as above.
Type safety at work: `mixData.getT2Value()` returns a `String` because the second parameter was declared `String`. Assign it to an `int` and the compiler stops you, no cast, no run-time surprise.
